content: Lead(II) nitrate is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula Pb(NO3)2. It typically appears as colorless crystals or a white powder and is water-soluble, unlike most other lead(II) salts. Historically known as plumb dulcis during the Middle Ages, it was produced on a small scale by reacting metallic lead or lead oxide with nitric acid, primarily for the synthesis of other lead compounds. By the 19th century, its production became commercialized in Europe and the United States. Its primary historical use was as a raw material for pigments in lead-based paints, such as chrome yellow and chrome orange. However, these paints have largely been replaced by less toxic alternatives like titanium dioxide-based paints. Other industrial applications included its use as a heat stabilizer in nylon and polyesters and as a coating for photothermographic paper. Since around 2000, lead(II) nitrate has also been used in gold cyanidation processes. Lead(II) nitrate is toxic, acts as an oxidizing agent, and is classified as probably carcinogenic to humans by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). Proper safety precautions are essential when handling this compound to prevent inhalation, ingestion, or skin contact. Its hazardous nature has led to scrutiny and limited applications. The compound dissolves readily in water, dissociating into lead(II) cations and nitrate anions. When mixed with iodide ions, it forms a bright orange-yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide, a reaction often used to demonstrate precipitation in educational settings. Lead(II) nitrate is one of the few water-soluble lead compounds, alongside lead(II) acetate. Most other lead compounds are insoluble in water. Its solubility makes it a key starting material for producing insoluble lead compounds through double decomposition reactions. The crystal structure of lead(II) nitrate has been determined using neutron diffraction. It crystallizes in a cubic system, with lead atoms in a face-centered cubic arrangement. Each lead atom is bonded to twelve oxygen atoms, and the nitrate groups are symmetrically arranged. Despite initial interest in the potential for free internal rotation of nitrate groups at elevated temperatures, this phenomenon was not observed. Lead(II) nitrate exhibits interesting supramolecular chemistry due to its ability to coordinate with nitrogen and oxygen electron-donating compounds. For example, combining lead nitrate with pentaethylene glycol in a solution of acetonitrile and methanol produces a crystalline material where the glycol chain wraps around the lead ion in a crown ether-like configuration. The coordination number in such complexes can reach up to 10, with the lead ion adopting a bicapped square antiprism geometry. These complexes are of academic interest and have potential applications. As an oxidizing agent, lead(II) nitrate decomposes upon heating to produce lead(II) oxide, oxygen, and nitrogen dioxide, accompanied by a crackling noise known as decrepitation. This property has been utilized in pyrotechnics, such as fireworks. Lead(II) nitrate is not naturally occurring and is typically synthesized by dissolving metallic lead or lead(II) oxide in nitric acid. The resulting solution, when concentrated, spontaneously forms anhydrous crystals of lead(II) nitrate. Commercially, it is available in various quantities, from laboratory-scale containers to industrial-sized bags. Impure solutions of lead(II) nitrate are also generated as by-products in the processing of lead-bismuth wastes from lead refineries and are used in gold cyanidation. Due to its toxicity, lead(II) nitrate has been largely replaced in many applications by safer alternatives. For example, its use in lead-based paints has been supplanted by titanium dioxide. Historical uses, such as in matches and fireworks, have also declined. Current applications include its use as a heat stabilizer in polymers, a coating for photothermographic paper, and in rodenticides. In laboratories, it serves as a reliable source of dinitrogen tetroxide when carefully dried and heated. Lead(II) nitrate is toxic and can cause acute lead poisoning if ingested. All inorganic lead compounds are classified as probably carcinogenic to humans (Category 2A) by the IARC. They have been linked to renal cancer, glioma, and other cancers in experimental animals, as well as renal, brain, and lung cancers in humans. Lead interferes with enzymes such as δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase in the heme biosynthetic pathway and pyrimidine-5'-nucleotidase, which is crucial for DNA metabolism. To minimize exposure, lead(II) nitrate must be handled in a fume hood with appropriate personal protective equipment. Spillage and environmental release must be avoided, and all materials and containers must be disposed of as hazardous waste.
